prompt:
## Harbor: the tide chart
The fabric cover around the folded tide chart is ochre, with a fine diagonal weave. This detail belongs to the existing object, stays at its established location and remains subordinate to the main action. Preserve its material and appearance through the camera movement.
The event takes place beside a small passenger ferry tied to a working harbor pier just before sunrise. An adult mechanic stands on the ferry's open side deck, and its captain stands beside the cabin entrance. The mechanic offers a folded tide chart and says, "The channel is clear." The captain accepts it, answers, "Then we can go," and looks out toward the harbor entrance. A slow lateral camera move reveals the channel beyond their shoulders. The boat remains moored throughout this brief exchange. Close voices, water against the hull, a loose halyard and a distant gull make the soundscape; there is no music.
The ferry is a practical coastal launch with a dark blue hull and a narrow cream band beneath its windows.
It carries a small enclosed cabin forward and an open passenger area behind it.
The camera is on the open deck, looking diagonally toward the cabin and the gap between the two people.
This angle places the pier along the left edge of the view and open water farther to the right.
The horizon is low enough that the upper part of the cabin has a clear silhouette against the pale sky.
Nothing in the composition suggests that the ferry is already underway.
The mechanic has finished a routine inspection rather than an emergency repair.
Their expression is alert but comfortable, with the slight tiredness of an early start.
They wear a plain work jacket over a warm shirt and carry no conspicuous badge or brand.
A few old creases in the jacket show where the elbows bend.
The sleeve nearest the chart has a darker damp patch near its cuff from resting against the rail.
Keep that patch in the same place as the arm moves.
The mechanic's free hand rests lightly on the top of a closed tool bag at hip level.
The captain is a different adult, dressed for a cool morning outside.
A heavy knit sweater is visible beneath an open weatherproof coat.
Their hair is tidy but not freshly styled, and the light catches a few loose strands when they turn toward the water.
Their stance is balanced on the gently moving deck, with one foot slightly ahead of the other.
They are listening to the mechanic before the first line begins.
The captain does not interrupt or make a broad theatrical gesture.
Their reply is a small decision shared between people accustomed to working together.
The tide chart is a real paper object with several old folds.
It is partly folded into a rectangle that can be held in one hand, but one narrow flap remains loose.
Faint printed lines and numbers are visible as a texture on its pale surface without becoming a readable title or a map inset.
A soft graphite mark near one fold suggests that it has been used for planning.
The mechanic holds its lower edge between the thumb and fingers, keeping the paper clear of the damp rail.
Its upper corner lifts slightly in the breeze before the captain takes it.
Begin with both people already in the frame.
The mechanic's hand and the chart occupy the space between their bodies, below their faces.
This arrangement lets the first line and the handover belong to the same view.
As the mechanic speaks, the chart moves a short distance toward the captain.
The motion is neither a flourish nor an abrupt thrust.
The captain's receiving hand rises from beside the coat, touches the opposite edge and supports it before the mechanic releases their grip.
The paper bends a little between the two hands during that shared moment of support.
The mechanic's line is spoken in an ordinary low voice suitable for the quiet morning. The consonants remain clear, but the delivery does not sound like a public announcement. Their mouth and jaw make the small movements of the exact words, and their eyes remain on the captain. There is a slight release of breath after "clear." The captain acknowledges the information with a very small nod before replying. The pause is long enough to register listening and short enough that the exchange feels familiar. Do not add another question, greeting or explanation of the voyage.
When the captain says, "Then we can go," the first part of the line is addressed to the mechanic. On the last words, their gaze begins to move toward the channel. The head follows the eyes through a modest turn, revealing more of the cheek nearest the exterior light. The chart settles against the front of the coat, still visibly held. The mechanic follows the captain's look with a quieter change of attention. Both remain in place. The ending is anticipation of departure, not departure itself: no engine surge, released rope or sudden movement of the ferry is needed.
The camera makes a restrained lateral movement toward the open-water side of the deck.
It travels only far enough for the gap between the people and the cabin edge to reveal more of the harbor entrance.
Keep the lens around chest-to-eye height, with a moderate field of view that gives both faces room.
This is a smooth observational move, not a circling orbit.
The cabin edge shifts more strongly against the distant breakwater than the breakwater shifts against the sky.
That small parallax is enough to make the depth of the harbor apparent.
The pier is built from old timber planks on dark vertical supports.
Its upper surface sits slightly higher than the ferry deck.
The planks run along the pier rather than across the direction of travel, with narrow uneven joints that collect moisture.
Near the edge, their color is darker where spray and repeated foot traffic have polished the grain.
A thin line of pale salt remains on a section that has dried under a small overhang.
The pier is not a freshly painted marina walkway.
Its modest wear should feel functional and maintained rather than picturesque decay.
A short gangplank connects the ferry to the pier behind the mechanic.
It remains still except for a barely perceptible change in angle as the boat moves against its lines.
Two narrow battens cross its surface to give shoes a purchase.
The upper end rests securely on the pier, and the lower end overlaps the ferry's boarding edge.
It should never detach or slide.
The gangplank can be partly obscured by the mechanic's body; its visible portion is enough to explain how the two surfaces connect.
No passenger needs to cross it during the exchange.
A thick mooring rope runs from a cleat near the ferry's edge toward a bollard on the pier.
Its direction is clear, and a small amount of tension holds it above the water.
A spare section lies in an orderly coil on the deck, away from the walking path.
The rope has a coarse twisted texture, with darker fibers where it is damp.
It may tighten or relax very slightly with the boat's slow movement, but it does not snap taut or drag its coil across the deck.
This quiet restraint helps establish that the vessel is secured.
The brass cleat has a broad base and two rounded horns.
It is attached firmly to the deck edge with visible fasteners whose heads sit flush.
The top is smoother and brighter where rope and hands have worn it, while the lower edges remain dull.
A small highlight follows the curve nearest the cabin light.
Do not make the whole fitting glow like gold.
The rope turns around it in a believable figure that leaves no impossible loop through solid metal.
Its shadow sits close to the deck and stays consistent while the camera moves past it.
Between the hull and the pier hangs a dark rubber fender on a short line.
It is partially hidden below the deck edge, with only its rounded upper section clearly visible.
Its surface is matte, slightly scuffed and wet near the bottom.
As the boat rests against it, it compresses subtly rather than behaving like a rigid barrel.
A faint rubber-on-wood contact can be heard once if the slow movement brings the surfaces together.
Keep that sound small.
The fender's purpose is practical protection, not a dramatic moving element that competes with the conversation.
The top rail along the open side of the ferry is painted steel, with a few small chips at the corners and near a frequently used handhold.
Its horizontal line gives the camera movement a steady reference.
The rail passes behind the captain's lower arm rather than through the body.
Where the chart crosses it in the image, the paper remains closer to the camera and separates clearly from the darker metal.
A few beads of moisture cling to the underside of the rail.
They can catch the sky light without turning into a continuous row of sparkling ornaments.
The cabin door is open only a short distance, enough to reveal warm interior light and a sliver of the wheelhouse.
Its blue paint is less weathered on the sheltered inner edge than on the exterior face.
The glass in its upper panel carries a faint reflection of the dawn sky.
Through that reflection, a dark shape of the steering wheel and the corner of a seat are suggested rather than shown in crisp detail.
The door is held in place and does not swing during the exchange.
Its stable angle explains the warm strip of light falling across the captain's coat.
The cabin interior is not a bright studio.
A small practical lamp illuminates the working area inside, leaving the ceiling and corners subdued.
A chart shelf, a narrow instrument panel and the outline of a folded cloth can be glimpsed through the opening.
None of the instruments needs a readable screen.
Any tiny indicator lights remain modest points rather than dominating the exposure.
The interior light is warmer than the morning outside, but it does not cast an orange wash across the entire deck.
Its influence is strongest near the doorway and fades naturally with distance.
The nearest cabin window has a thin metal frame and a dark rubber gasket.
A few dried traces of salt on the lower part of the glass soften its reflection.
The sky appears as a pale cool patch near the top, while the pier is reflected more darkly below.
When the captain turns, the glass may show only a vague moving tone, not a second sharply rendered face looking in a different direction.
Preserve the window's rectangular shape and its relation to the door.
The frame should not bend as though it were part of a flexible curtain.
A simple passenger bench runs along the cabin wall behind the captain.
Its slats are painted a worn cream color that echoes the band on the hull.
The seat is empty, with a narrow line of moisture along its outer edge.
Its supporting brackets are dark and mostly in shadow.
The bench provides a horizontal layer below the cabin windows and a clue to the ferry's everyday use.
Do not place luggage or additional people on it.
Its quiet presence leaves the deck clear for the two workers and makes the early hour believable.
The mechanic's tool bag is a compact canvas bag with a reinforced base.
Its mouth is closed loosely enough that the handle of a screwdriver and the edge of a folded rag are visible.
The bag rests on a stable low support beside the mechanic rather than hanging unsupported from the hand.
Its canvas is faded and creased, with a darker bottom from repeated use.
The hand resting on it slightly depresses the soft top.
There is no spill of tools and no new repair action; the bag belongs to the inspection that has already been completed before this moment.
A raised hatch rim lies farther along the deck, outside the path of the handover.
The hatch itself is closed, with a shallow channel around its edge that catches a little water.
Its metal surface carries scuffs in several directions from shoes and equipment.
A small latch sits flat.
This detail should not suggest that an unseen person is about to emerge from below.
It is simply part of the vessel's working layout.
In the lateral camera movement, the hatch changes position against the bench in a way consistent with its lower and nearer location.
The deck has a nonslip painted surface with fine roughness visible near the camera.
Its color is a muted gray-green, darker in damp patches.
Small puddles collect where the surface dips slightly near a seam.
The largest visible puddle is shallow enough to preserve the texture beneath it, and its reflection trembles with the motion of the vessel.
Do not make the whole deck ankle-deep in water.
The workers' shoes remain dry above the soles, and their movements produce no exaggerated splashes.
A soft sole adjustment can make a faint damp squeak or rub.
The water immediately beside the ferry is darker than the open harbor because the hull and pier shade it.
Small waves lift and fall against the curved side, breaking its reflection into vertical fragments.
A pale strip of sky occasionally appears between those fragments.
The water is not rough enough to throw spray onto the people.
Its motion is a slow irregular pattern caused by the harbor's background movement, not by an active propeller.
There is no foaming wake behind the boat.
Keep the sound correspondingly gentle, with separate small laps and a low watery wash.
Farther from the hull, the harbor surface opens into a broad cool plane.
Low ripples catch more of the sky and become lighter toward the channel.
The reflections of distant structures stretch and break across that surface, with enough variation to show that the water is moving.
A small floating fragment can drift in the middle distance without becoming a subject.
The horizon remains level, except for the very slight shared motion of the boat and camera.
Do not make distant buildings rock independently while the people and deck remain perfectly still.
Across the harbor stands a low warehouse with a pitched roof and a row of closed loading doors.
Its walls are a subdued gray-brown, softened by the distance and morning air.
One small exterior light remains on near a doorway.
The roofline is uneven in the ordinary way of a working waterfront, with a short vent and a gutter visible against the sky.
The warehouse should not become a dramatic industrial skyline.
It establishes the scale of the harbor and the fact that work will soon begin, while staying visually quieter than the people in the foreground.
A closed ticket booth sits on the pier behind the gangplank.
Only part of its small roof and shuttered front need be visible.
A narrow board beneath the window holds a faded timetable whose lettering is too distant to read.
The booth has no illuminated advertisement or animated display.
Its door is shut, and no attendant appears.
A small metal latch and the edge of a rain gutter give it a practical character.
The booth helps identify the ferry as a passenger vessel without requiring a sign that announces the scene's purpose.
On the pier near that booth, a short stack of empty crates is pushed against a wall.
Their slatted sides and open tops make their construction clear, but they remain away from the gangplank.
They are not full of fish or moving animals.
A folded cover lies over the upper crate, weighted at one corner.
The cover's loose edge can move slightly in the same breeze that lifts the paper chart.
This repeated direction of small wind-driven motion connects different parts of the setting without turning the wind into a strong force.
The harbor entrance is defined by two low breakwater arms that leave a clear opening in the distance.
One arm is more visible than the other from this camera angle.
Its stones or concrete blocks form a low dark line, with a small navigation marker near the end.
The opening leads toward a slightly brighter strip of water beneath the pale sky.
This is the destination of the captain's final look.
Do not place a large ship in the opening or make the marker flash dramatically at the moment of the reply.
The channel is simply open and calm.
A distant navigation pole carries a small muted signal light.
Its color can be recognized as a maritime marker without becoming a bright visual cue timed to the dialogue.
The pole remains vertical and fixed to its base.
A faint reflection may appear on the water beneath it, broken by ripples and much less saturated than the light itself.
The marker's apparent size is small compared with the cabin fittings in the foreground.
It should remain part of the depth of the harbor rather than appearing as a large object immediately behind the captain.
The sky is clear enough to show a gradual transition from cool blue above to a pale warm-gray band near the horizon.
The sun itself has not yet risen into the frame.
Thin cloud near the water can soften that transition without forming a spectacular sunset pattern.
The overall illumination is calm and low in contrast.
Faces remain readable through the broad sky light and the nearby cabin reflection.
Avoid a sudden beam of golden sunlight crossing the deck during the few seconds of the exchange; the light should belong to one stable moment before sunrise.
The breeze is light and comes from the open-water side toward the pier.
It moves a loose corner of the chart, a few strands of hair and the edge of the cover on the crates in broadly consistent directions.
Heavy coats and the mooring rope do not flap vigorously.
A hanging halyard on a neighboring mast can tap its support intermittently.
The breeze is more evident through these small consequences than through a loud wind sound in the microphone.
Keep speech clear and do not add the distorted buffeting of a microphone exposed to a storm.
The halyard belongs to a vessel outside the principal frame, slightly behind and to the left of the listening position.
Its sound is a light irregular tap against a mast, with small changes in spacing rather than a metronomic rhythm.
It should remain quieter than the voices and the nearest water.
The source does not need to be revealed by a pan.
It helps make the harbor extend beyond the visible ferry.
If a thin mast line is visible in the distance, it should remain associated with a moored boat and not drift freely through the sky.
A gull is heard once from farther out in the harbor.
Its call is brief and carries an open outdoor quality rather than a close harsh squawk.
A small bird may be visible on a distant post, but the sound does not require a close-up or a perfectly synchronized beak animation at that distance.
The call should not interrupt either spoken line.
It can sit in the pause or under the ambient water.
Avoid introducing a flock circling around the people; the scene's attention remains with their quiet preparation for departure.
The water sound nearest the camera has several layers: a low wash under the deck edge, a small hollow lap where water meets the hull, and occasional lighter movement against the pier supports.
These layers are related but not identical loops.
Their levels vary modestly as a ripple arrives and recedes.
A slight creak from a mooring fitting can accompany the ferry's restrained movement.
Do not add a loud ship's horn, an engine rev or a chain being hauled, because none of those actions occurs in the visible moment.
The ferry's machinery contributes only a subdued background hum if one is audible at all.
It should feel like equipment idling or an electrical system already on, not a powerful engine accelerating.
The hum is steadier and lower than the halyard taps.
It remains behind the conversation and does not rise when the captain says they can go.
This distinction matters to the ending: the words express readiness, while the boat has not yet begun its departure procedure.
The audience can anticipate movement beyond the clip without seeing or hearing it start.
The chart produces a small dry paper sound as the grip changes.
That sound is close enough to have a little crispness, softened by the cool damp air and the hands touching it.
The loose flap settles against the folded body of the chart after the captain receives it.
A sleeve brushes the coat lightly as the receiving arm returns toward the torso.
These are small foley details, not prominent effects.
They should be audible only in proportion to the quietness of the harbor and should not replace the continuous environmental bed beneath them.
The two voices have different natural timbres.
The mechanic's voice can be slightly rougher from the early hour, while the captain's reply is a little more resonant.
Both sound close to one another and to the camera, without studio-like isolation.
Their speech reflects faintly from the cabin wall but mostly opens into the harbor air.
Keep the exact words intelligible.
There is no unseen narrator describing what the chart means, and no radio voice giving navigation instructions in the background.
The scene's meaning comes from the exchange and the final direction of attention.
The mechanic's eyes remain attentive during the handover.
A brief downward glance checks the captain's grip, then the gaze returns to the face.
After the reply, the mechanic can shift weight slightly toward the rail without taking a step.
The free hand remains near the tool bag.
This small recovery makes the person feel present beyond the line of dialogue.
It should not introduce a new task, such as opening the bag, adjusting machinery or untying the ferry.
The event remains one completed exchange of information and paper.
The captain's receiving hand is visible long enough to show that the chart has changed owners.
The fingers close around the paper before it comes to rest against the coat.
The captain does not unfold the entire chart during the clip.
Keeping it partly folded lets the handover remain simple and leaves room for the final look toward the channel.
The coat sleeve forms a short diagonal from the elbow to the hand, separating the pale chart from the darker torso.
That clear shape should survive the lateral camera move and the head turn.
The distance between the two people is comfortable for conversation and a short reach.
Neither needs to lean far across the deck or stretch an arm to its limit.
Their bodies are angled slightly toward one another, leaving an open triangular gap through which the camera can glimpse the water.
As the camera moves, the gap changes modestly but does not disappear.
The captain's turn opens it a little more at the ending.
Use this simple blocking to reveal the harbor naturally, rather than moving either person out of the frame solely to expose a background view.
Keep the ferry's movement subtle enough that the handover is easy.
The deck and the people share a slow, small motion against the fixed pier.
The workers make unconscious balance adjustments through their knees and ankles, not large sways.
The cabin, bench and rail remain rigidly connected to the deck.
The mooring line and fender explain the limits of the boat's motion.
Avoid making the camera independently bob in a different rhythm; it is observing from the same vessel and should inherit much of that shared movement.
The nearest wet surfaces receive two different kinds of reflection.
The broad cool sky produces soft light across the rail and deck, while the cabin lamp creates a smaller warmer patch near the doorway.
The warm patch should not spread across the far side of the ferry without a reflective path.
On the chart, the paper remains mostly cool and pale, with a slight warm influence near the captain's hand if it approaches the doorway.
The faces can show this same mixture gently, preserving believable skin color rather than strong blue-and-orange theatrical contrast.
The overall composition should feel occupied by work without being cluttered.
Keep the path from the gangplank to the cabin clear.
Place the tool bag outside that path and the spare rope coil near its cleat.
The empty passenger bench stays available for later use.
The chart is the only loose object being actively handled.
This practical arrangement makes the ferry believable as a vessel preparing for passengers, and it prevents small props from becoming arbitrary obstacles around the workers' feet.
Small marks of maintenance can appear where they make sense.
A rail corner may have a newer patch of paint, a hatch seal may look cleaner than the surrounding metal, and a replacement board on the pier may be slightly lighter than its neighbors.
These details suggest care over time without implying that the ferry is unsafe or derelict.
They remain stationary and modest.
Do not turn chipped paint into spreading damage or make a repaired surface change color while the camera passes it.
The background remains quiet throughout the exchange.
A distant moored boat can show a small mast or cabin shape beyond the pier, but it does not pull away or cross the channel.
The warehouse doors stay closed.
The ticket booth remains unoccupied.
A navigation marker and the breakwater give a fixed destination to the captain's look.
These stable elements let the foreground paper, faces and gentle water movement carry the scene.
The harbor feels ready to wake rather than already crowded with simultaneous departures.
At the final moment, the camera has revealed slightly more open water while still retaining the captain, the chart and part of the mechanic in the composition.
The captain's face is turned enough to show the direction of attention but not so far that the expression disappears entirely.
The mechanic remains quietly beside them.
Let a small lap of water and the natural decay of the last spoken word continue.
End before anyone reaches for a control or a mooring line.
The shared readiness is the resolution of this scene.
Treat the scene as a photographed event with a definite place for the camera, the subjects and each sound source.
The detailed description supplies information about the same moment from several perspectives.
It does not ask for an additional shot every time a surface, gesture or sound is mentioned.
Follow only the cuts and camera movements explicitly named in the scene description.
Details outside the frame still explain the light or sound reaching the camera, but they do not require an insert shot.
The final image should feel like a coherent observation rather than a succession of illustrations of individual nouns.
Choose an exposure that keeps the main subject readable while preserving the direction of the available light.
A face turned away from a window should become darker on that side.
Do not compensate by introducing a second bright light that has no source in the setting.
Small bright reflections can approach white, particularly on polished metal or wet surfaces, but broad areas of skin, cloth and painted material should retain their color.
Deep recesses may remain dark.
The viewer should be able to distinguish a shadowed surface from an empty hole without every part of the setting receiving the same brightness.
Maintain a consistent white balance throughout each continuous shot.
A warm practical lamp and a cool exterior opening can both remain visible as different sources of illumination.
Their colors should mix gradually on surfaces that receive both.
A subject moving between those sources may change in color naturally, while a stationary neutral object keeps its established appearance.
Avoid a global color shift whenever a brighter object crosses the frame.
The scene's chosen palette comes from its materials and lighting rather than from a uniform colored veil placed over the image.
The camera has one plausible lens for each described view.
Straight architectural edges near the center remain straight, while any mild wide-angle stretching belongs near the edge of a wide composition.
An object should not change its proportions merely because it becomes important to the action.
During a lateral move, nearby edges travel across the picture faster than distant ones.
The background opens or closes through gaps in the foreground according to that movement.
Preserve this depth information even when the camera's travel is small; it gives the setting a volume rather than the appearance of a painted backdrop.
Focus should help the viewer follow the principal action.
Establish a clear plane around the important face, hands, instrument or animal, as appropriate to the scene.
Objects farther away can soften gradually, without an abrupt cutout around the subject.
A foreground object crossing the lens may briefly become a large soft shape.
Its blur should still carry the object's approximate color and orientation.
If the described action calls for attention to move between subjects, let any focus change happen once, deliberately, and over a visible interval.
Do not hunt repeatedly between unrelated background details.
Keep the camera's height understandable.
A view from standing eye level sees the tops of low objects and the underside of high overhangs in a consistent way.
A close view of hands may place the lens lower, but the horizon and background lines should agree with that position.
A tilt changes which part of the setting enters the frame; it does not make the floor rise like a hinged panel.
When the scene calls for an upward or downward movement, retain a recognizable stationary edge long enough for the viewer to understand that the camera is moving through a stable place.
Allow motion blur to come from movement rather than from a general softening of the frame.
A quick hand, falling droplet, drumstick or wing can leave a short directional trace during its fastest movement.
A stationary wall behind it should remain stationary.
The blur follows the object's actual path and becomes shorter as it slows.
A turning object can have a sharp center and a more blurred extremity.
Do not turn a brief fast gesture into slow motion unless the scene specifically calls for that treatment; the timing of its sound must continue to agree with its visible speed.
Preserve the continuity of a body through partial occlusion.
If one hand passes behind a bowl, railing or instrument, its hidden movement should lead to a plausible reappearance on the other side.
Keep the wrist attached to the same forearm, with the sleeve ending at a stable location.
When a person turns, the far shoulder narrows and the near shoulder broadens according to the turn.
Clothing folds can change, but seams, cuffs, buttons and the major color blocks remain associated with the same garment.
Do not replace an obscured limb with a new pose disconnected from the movement that preceded it.
A grasp should look like contact with a particular object, not a hand hovering around an approximate shape.
Place the thumb on one side and the fingers on the other when the object permits that grip.
Show a small adjustment before a transfer of weight if the action requires it.
A flexible object can bend where pressure is applied; a rigid object keeps its shape.
When the grip relaxes, the fingers separate in a natural sequence.
The object remains supported by the other hand, a surface or its own attachment rather than pausing unsupported in the air.
The main action has preparation, contact and recovery, even when those phases are brief.
A person shifts balance before leaning over a work surface.
A wrist turns before a tool changes direction.
An animal compresses or extends its body before a leap.
These small anticipations should remain subordinate to the action, not become a separate performance.
After contact, the body absorbs the force through an appropriate joint or support.
A movement should not end in a perfectly frozen pose while loose clothing, water or a suspended object still has momentum that would visibly continue.
Keep feet and supports meaningful when they are in view.
A standing person's weight is carried through the soles rather than through a floating outline above the ground.
If the upper body leans, the ankles, knees or hips make a corresponding adjustment.
A seated subject remains related to the seat beneath them, with cloth compressed at points of contact.
The legs of a stool or table meet the floor at consistent locations.
Small contact shadows help describe this relationship.
Do not move the floor texture beneath a stationary support to create the impression of camera motion.
Let the face communicate the stated mood through small changes in the eyes, mouth and posture.
An attentive look can involve a brief eye movement before the head follows.
A restrained smile should develop through the cheeks and corners of the mouth rather than appearing as an entirely new expression in one frame.
Skin has modest variation in color and texture, with a softer reflection than polished objects in the same light.
Preserve the person's facial proportions as their expression changes.
A turn away from the camera can hide part of the face without replacing the visible profile.
For spoken words, align the visible articulation with the voice of the person who is speaking.
The other person can listen, breathe or react without mimicking the same syllables.
Short pauses between lines should feel like an exchange of attention rather than a gap in the soundtrack.
A speaker may begin a word while looking at an object and finish while glancing toward the listener.
Keep the voice at a natural conversational level for the distance between them.
The specified line is sufficient; do not fill remaining time with additional dialogue, narration or an unrelated exclamation.
Background people, when the scene contains them, should have quieter and less complete gestures than the principal subjects.
A distant passerby can continue along a visible path, and someone at a neighboring activity can make a small ordinary movement.
Their behavior should support the setting without forming a second competing scene.
Keep their apparent size consistent with their distance.
A person behind a doorway or a railing should remain behind that obstruction.
If the scene is explicitly unoccupied except for its main subjects, do not add a crowd simply to make the frame busier.
Describe materials through the way they respond to light and contact.
Worn wood has a grain that follows the object, with smoother areas where hands have polished it.
Painted metal may have a broad colored reflection and small chips exposing a different material beneath.
Fabric scatters light across its weave and gathers into folds near tension points.
Glass transmits a view with reflections superimposed on it.
These responses should distinguish neighboring objects without exaggerating every surface into a showcase texture.
Details become quieter with distance and remain attached to their physical surfaces during motion.
Water follows the slope and movement of the surface carrying it.
A bead on a tilted edge can lengthen, detach and fall; it should not move upward without an external force.
Ripples spread from a contact point and interact with existing water motion.
A reflection on moving water breaks into related patches rather than remaining a rigid duplicate of the reflected object.
Where water wets a porous surface, the material can darken and lose some of its dry texture.
Keep such changes localized to the area that actually receives the water.
Airborne material should have a clear origin.
Steam rises from heat and becomes less dense as it mixes with cooler air.
Dust can remain briefly suspended after a contact that lifts it.
A small spray begins at a splash or wet movement and separates into droplets of different sizes.
Do not introduce a continuous cloud that has no source.
The material can veil an object behind it, but the object remains in place and reappears with the same form when the veil thins.
Its softness comes from transparency and depth, not from erasing the background.
Reflections must agree with the scene's positions.
A window can reflect a light behind the camera while revealing a darker interior beyond its glass.
A curved metal surface compresses and bends the reflected environment.
A puddle reflects the sky or an object at an appropriate angle; it does not show the camera's entire view as though it were a second screen.
When an object moves, its reflection changes in relation to the reflecting surface.
If the reflection disappears at an edge or behind a ripple, the object itself should not disappear with it.
Shadows help identify the placement of light sources.
A broad source creates a softer transition, especially when an object is separated from the surface receiving its shadow.
A small nearby source can create a more definite shape.
Where the object touches its support, the contact shadow becomes compact and dark.
Multiple sources may weaken or tint a shadow without making its direction arbitrary.
Let a moving hand or tool change the shadow on nearby surfaces as it passes, while the shadows of fixed structures stay consistent with the established illumination.
Keep fine patterns quiet enough to belong to the scene.
Cloth weave, mesh, rope fibers, bark and closely spaced rails should not flicker between unrelated arrangements as the camera moves.
A pattern can lose detail with distance or motion, but its overall spacing and direction remain stable.
Printed markings, if present, stay on the same object and follow its perspective.
Unless the scene explicitly asks for legible writing, background text can remain an ordinary indistinct part of the setting.
Do not invent title cards, subtitles, brand marks or explanatory diagrams over the picture.
The stereo soundscape should have a stable center of attention.
Place the principal voice or central action near its visible position, with smaller changes in balance as the camera or subject moves.
A sound from the left side of the setting can favor that side without disappearing from the other channel completely.
The room or outdoor ambience occupies a broader space.
Avoid moving every sound across the stereo field merely because the camera pans; its acoustic position depends on the source and listening perspective, not on an arbitrary visual effect.
Separate close foley from distant ambience by clarity and proportion.
A hand touching a tool can produce a small crisp detail close to the listener.
A distant vehicle, bird or conversation arrives with less high-frequency definition and a lower level.
Keep the background continuous enough to establish the place, but leave room for a quiet spoken line or important contact sound.
The scene does not need an exaggerated sound for every visible movement.
Some motions, especially distant or gentle ones, can remain inaudible beneath the environment's existing sound bed.
Match a contact sound to the instant of contact.
A tap begins when the moving object reaches the receiving surface, not while it is still approaching.
A splash begins when the body or object breaks the water.
A percussion strike has a sharp beginning followed by the resonant character of the instrument.
A motor or continuous friction sound can begin before the shot and persist through it.
Do not restart a continuous sound each time the camera cuts back to the object producing it.
Let the visible action and the sound share the same physical cause.
The character of a sound should come from the materials involved.
Wood can produce a short dry knock, thin metal a brighter ring, cloth a soft rustle, and damp contact a quieter low friction sound.
A large resonant object may continue vibrating after the initial strike.
Nearby soft materials can absorb part of that tail.
Keep the sound small when the motion is small; a fingertip adjustment should not sound like a heavy impact.
Distinct sources should remain distinguishable without turning each one into an isolated effect played at full volume.
Use reverberation to describe the enclosure.
A hard-walled interior can return a restrained early reflection after a voice or tap.
A courtyard may create a short reflection from nearby walls while remaining open above.
A woodland stream or open harbor usually has a more diffuse outdoor character, with sound fading into the environment rather than returning as a large indoor echo.
Do not put the same spacious hall reverberation on every source.
The distance to nearby boundaries and the presence of soft materials should shape the acoustic impression.
Preserve low-level room tone or environmental noise during pauses in the main action.
The soundscape should not drop to absolute silence between words or impacts unless silence itself is specifically part of the scene.
A slight breath, distant water, an electrical hum or air moving through leaves can make the pause feel inhabited.
Keep that bed modest and stable.
It should not swell dramatically to fill every gap, and it should not become a musical drone unless music is explicitly called for in the scene description.
When music is absent, let rhythm come from the physical activity and environment.
Repeated tools, footsteps, water or machinery may produce patterns without turning into an added score.
When the scene contains musicians, their audible performance belongs to their visible instruments and gestures.
Keep the number and character of those instruments consistent with the performers present.
A lingering resonance after a final beat is natural; a new unseen orchestra entering at the ending is not.
Preserve the scene's chosen distinction between performed sound and background music.
The overall mix should allow the viewer to understand what is happening without sounding artificially isolated.
A voice can sit above a moderate environmental bed while still sharing its space.
A loud brief action can mask quieter details for an instant, then allow them to emerge again.
Do not hold a background effect at an unnaturally fixed level through every foreground event.
Keep abrupt level changes tied to a plausible source, such as a motor stopping or a door opening.
The final tail should retain the acoustic character established at the beginning.
If the scene contains a cut, carry through the physical state of the event.
The object held before the cut remains in the same hand afterward.
A person does not change clothes or reverse their place in the setting.
An ongoing sound can bridge the cut and help connect the views.
A closer shot reveals detail that was already part of the wider scene rather than introducing a new version of the object.
The cut should clarify the described action, and the sequence should contain only the views specified in the scene brief.
Keep screen direction understandable across those views.
If two people face one another, retain their established left-right relationship unless the camera visibly crosses to the other side.
A moving object that exits toward one side should enter the next view in a direction consistent with the shared space.
The viewer should not need an unexplained reversal to understand a simple handover, gesture or tool movement.
A small change in angle is enough to reveal depth; it does not require the entire setting to rotate around the subjects.
At the beginning, the event can already be underway.
A wheel may already be turning, water already moving, or a musician already holding the position needed for the next beat.
Establish enough context in the first image that the main action is immediately legible.
Avoid spending most of the clip on an empty establishing view if the scene asks for a brief exchange or quick movement.
The setting's detail should be available within the composition while the event proceeds, rather than delaying the event until every object has been introduced.
At the ending, let the action reach its stated small resolution.
A received object rests in the new holder's hand; a final beat resonates; a returning animal settles; a tool stops where the worker intends it to stop.
The environment can continue moving beyond that resolution.
Hold the final relationship long enough to read it without adding a second incident.
There is no need for a fade, a logo, an explanatory caption or a dramatic new camera move.
End with the same world still present around the subjects.
The emotional tone should arise from the described behavior.
Quiet concentration can be conveyed through deliberate attention and economical movement.
Enjoyment can appear in a brief shared glance or a relaxed recovery after a successful action.
A natural event can be compelling without making the animal perform a human expression.
Avoid enlarging a restrained scene into a melodramatic confrontation or celebration.
The viewer should feel close to an ordinary moment whose textures, sounds and physical details make it worth watching.
Use background detail to support this tone.
A working place may show wear, repairs, stored tools and traces of repeated use, but it need not become dirty or neglected.
A natural place can include uneven growth and debris without looking arranged for decoration.
An organized surface can still have small asymmetries.
Let these details belong to the activity and location rather than scattering unrelated objects to fill empty space.
A few clear relationships between the people, their work and the setting are more valuable than a frame in which every surface competes for attention.
Keep the image free from unexplained graphic effects.
Light can flare modestly when a bright source approaches the lens, but it should not produce decorative streaks unrelated to that source.
A shallow depth of field can soften a background without cutting the subject out against a featureless wash.
Grain, if visible, remains fine and unobtrusive.
The scene's realism comes from consistent observation of light, material, movement and sound; it does not require an artificial cinematic overlay or a conspicuous filter announcing a style separate from the event.
Throughout the clip, preserve the hierarchy of attention established by the scene.
The main action is clearest, the immediate surroundings explain it, and the more distant setting gives it a place in the world.
A small incidental detail can become briefly noticeable when light or motion reveals it, then return to the background.
Do not let incidental motion interrupt the only spoken line or conceal the decisive gesture.
All of the detailed directions belong to this one hierarchy and should combine into a readable, continuous experience.
Consider the space just beyond each edge of the picture as a continuation of the visible setting.
A wall that exits the frame still explains the light reflected onto a nearby face.
A stream entering from the distance carries water from a place beyond the composition.
A work surface continues far enough to support the tools partly hidden at its edge.
Do not bend these surfaces toward the lens simply to show every named detail.
Partial visibility is natural when the camera occupies one definite position.
The scene remains understandable because the visible portions agree with one another.
Where the foreground and background have similar colors, separate them through ordinary optical cues.
A near edge may be sharper, a distant surface may receive softer light, and a contact shadow may reveal a small gap.
Do not draw an artificial bright outline around the subject.
If two dark forms overlap, allow some of that overlap to remain quiet rather than forcing every boundary to maximum contrast.
The most important contacts need clarity; less important background junctions can be ambiguous in the normal way a photographed place is ambiguous when viewed briefly.
Use negative space as part of the action's readability.
A hand needs a little clear area in the direction it is about to move, and a diving bird needs visible water below its perch.
This does not mean centering every object or distributing props symmetrically.
The free space should follow the scene's physical task.
When the action occupies that space, the composition can become denser for a moment and then open again during recovery.
Preserve the setting behind it so this change feels like movement through a place rather than a rearrangement of graphic elements.
The brightest region of the frame need not always be the protagonist.
A window, sky opening or lamp can be brighter while the subject remains readable through shape, placement and movement.
Control the size of those bright regions so they do not overwhelm the action.
A small reflection can attract the eye briefly and then recede as its angle changes.
Broad highlights should retain enough shape to identify their source.
Avoid automatic-looking exposure pumping that darkens a face whenever a reflective object passes through the composition.
Let shadows have different degrees of softness according to the light source and distance to the receiving surface.
A broad window gives a soft edge, while a small nearby lamp can make a more defined one.
Contact shadows are tighter than shadows cast across a larger gap.
On a curved receiver, the shadow changes shape with the surface.
If several sources contribute, their shadows can overlap with unequal darkness.
This physical variety helps explain depth without applying the same dark border to every object in the scene.
Reflected color should be local.
A warm wooden counter can return a little warmth to the underside of a hand above it.
Green foliage can tint a shaded patch near a stream.
Red task lighting can color nearby metal while a distant opening remains cool.
Keep these influences weaker than direct illumination unless the scene explicitly places the subject close to a large colored surface.
The reflected tint belongs to the facing side of an object and changes gradually with distance, rather than replacing the object's base color across its whole visible area.
Fine details should obey the scale of the view.
A close hand can show a crease near a knuckle, while a distant face needs only its stable overall proportions and expression.
The grain of a nearby wooden tool may be visible, but the far wall does not need equally sharp pores.
As the camera moves, details become available through a change of angle or distance rather than appearing as random new marks.
Preserve the few distinctive features that identify an object, and let less important texture merge naturally when it is too small to resolve.
When a reflective surface turns, its highlight can travel faster than a mark painted on it.
The highlight is an image of a light source seen through the changing surface orientation, while the mark belongs to the material.
Keep that distinction on wet clay, metal rims, glass and water.
A highlight may disappear at an angle where the source is no longer reflected.
It should not leave a permanent bright stain behind.
Conversely, a scratch or chip does not slide across the object merely because the camera changes position.
Translucent edges should retain their own thickness and texture.
A leaf against the light may show a warmer or brighter rim, and thin paper can glow softly near a lamp.
Steam can reveal an object behind it with reduced contrast.
These are different kinds of transmission and should not share one identical blur effect.
Keep opaque supports opaque.
A hand behind steam remains a solid hand glimpsed through moving vapor; it does not become transparent itself.
When the vapor clears, the same hand occupies the same physical place.
The action's pace should fit ordinary human or animal movement at its stated scale.
A small precise adjustment takes less travel than a broad gesture but can still have a deliberate beginning and ending.
Do not stretch a short line of dialogue into unnatural syllables merely to occupy the clip.
Let quiet anticipation and recovery provide breathing room where appropriate.
A fast event can happen within a calmer surrounding interval.
The scene's detail describes what is present during that interval, rather than requiring each noun to receive its own separate time allocation.
For scenes with speech, give the sentence an intention appropriate to the relationship.
A practical instruction can be clear without being stern; a question can be curious without sounding anxious; a calm reply can be warm without becoming sentimental.
Preserve the exact specified words while allowing natural stress, breath and a small pause where the phrase requires it.
The listener's response begins from understanding the line, not from mechanically copying the speaker's mouth.
Environmental sound continues underneath, maintaining the shared location of both people.
In scenes without speech, resist the urge to supply explanatory vocalizations.
Allow the last small movement to settle within the established composition, with the environmental sound continuing around it. Preserve the established framing as the scene reaches its stated resolution.

prompt:
In a quiet pottery studio an adult potter steadies a small spinning bowl while an adult apprentice watches. The apprentice asks, "Is the rim ready?" The potter says, "One more gentle pass," and smooths the lip with a damp sponge. Begin with a close view of the hands, then make one restrained cut to a shoulder-level view showing both faces. The wheel hum, damp clay, a light splash and breathing form the soundscape. The movement is careful and unhurried, with no background music. The entire event is one finishing pass on the same bowl, not a demonstration of the whole pottery process.
The apprentice's apron pocket is indigo, with a broad central stripe. This detail belongs to the existing object, stays at its established location and remains subordinate to the main action. Preserve its material and appearance through the camera movement.
The wheel sits near a tall north-facing window on the left wall of the studio.
Its circular splash pan is at the seated potter's waist.
The apprentice stands beyond the right side of the wheel, with enough room between their clothes and the wet rim to avoid accidental contact.
Behind the potter, a shallow shelf holds a few dry cups.
A sink is farther back on the right, beneath a small rack of towels.
These positions remain fixed through the cut.
The wider view reveals the same work area that surrounds the hands in the opening close view.
The bowl is modest in size, comfortably held between two hands.
Its side rises from a low foot in a continuous shallow curve and ends in a slightly thickened lip.
The clay is warm gray with a brown undertone, darker where it is wet.
A narrow spiral line below the rim records the potter's earlier touch.
That line rotates with the bowl, while a stationary highlight from the window travels over the passing surface.
Keep these two motions distinguishable: the material marks belong to the clay, and the reflected light belongs to the relationship between the surface and the window.
Open with the camera low enough to see the bowl's interior without looking directly down onto the wheel.
The potter's left fingertips support the inside edge.
The right hand holds a small natural sponge outside the lip.
Neither hand blocks the whole form.
The near edge of the splash pan occupies the bottom of the composition as a soft curved boundary.
Beyond the hands, the apprentice's apron is initially out of focus.
This arrangement gives the close shot depth and prepares the later view of the two people without requiring another establishing shot.
The left hand is already stable when the clip begins.
Its fingers form a loose supportive curve rather than squeezing the wall.
The sponge approaches the outside edge with only a small adjustment of the wrist.
As it contacts the clay, it compresses slightly and darkens where moisture gathers.
The bowl continues to rotate at a steady moderate speed.
Show the finishing pass as a change in the surface's smoothness and the evenness of the lip, not as a large change in the bowl's overall shape.
The work is nearly finished before this moment begins.
The apprentice asks the question while looking at the rim, then briefly lifts their eyes toward the potter.
Their hands rest loosely together in front of the apron, safely away from the rotating work.
The question is curious and quiet, with the natural upward inflection of someone checking a detail.
The potter answers without stopping the wheel or turning their whole body.
A small glance toward the apprentice is sufficient before attention returns to the clay.
Keep the spoken words exactly as given, with no narrator explaining the technique and no extra exchange after the answer.
Cut once after the question has made the apprentice's presence clear.
The shoulder-level view places the potter to the left and the apprentice to the right, preserving the established relation to the wheel.
The bowl remains visible between them in the lower part of the frame.
The potter's right hand still holds the same sponge at the same point on the rim.
Continue the wheel sound across the cut without a restart.
The change of view should feel like a closer understanding of the same instant, not a jump forward to a later stage of the work.
The potter wears a practical cotton work shirt with the sleeves rolled above the wrists.
The folds gather at the elbows and remain dry there.
Small clay marks on the forearms and apron are concentrated near the work area.
They do not spread or migrate during the pass.

Enjoyment can appear in a brief shared glance or a relaxed recovery after a successful action.
A natural event can be compelling without making the animal perform a human expression.
Avoid enlarging a restrained scene into a melodramatic confrontation or celebration.
The viewer should feel close to an ordinary moment whose textures, sounds and physical details make it worth watching.
Use background detail to support this tone.
A working place may show wear, repairs, stored tools and traces of repeated use, but it need not become dirty or neglected.
A natural place can include uneven growth and debris without looking arranged for decoration.
An organized surface can still have small asymmetries.
Let these details belong to the activity and location rather than scattering unrelated objects to fill empty space.
A few clear relationships between the people, their work and the setting are more valuable than a frame in which every surface competes for attention.
Keep the image free from unexplained graphic effects.
Light can flare modestly when a bright source approaches the lens, but it should not produce decorative streaks unrelated to that source.
A shallow depth of field can soften a background without cutting the subject out against a featureless wash.
Grain, if visible, remains fine and unobtrusive.
The scene's realism comes from consistent observation of light, material, movement and sound; it does not require an artificial cinematic overlay or a conspicuous filter announcing a style separate from the event.
Throughout the clip, preserve the hierarchy of attention established by the scene.
The main action is clearest, the immediate surroundings explain it, and the more distant setting gives it a place in the world.
A small incidental detail can become briefly noticeable when light or motion reveals it, then return to the background.
Do not let incidental motion interrupt the only spoken line or conceal the decisive gesture.
All of the detailed directions belong to this one hierarchy and should combine into a readable, continuous experience.
Consider the space just beyond each edge of the picture as a continuation of the visible setting.
A wall that exits the frame still explains the light reflected onto a nearby face.
A stream entering from the distance carries water from a place beyond the composition.
A work surface continues far enough to support the tools partly hidden at its edge.
Do not bend these surfaces toward the lens simply to show every named detail.
Partial visibility is natural when the camera occupies one definite position.
The scene remains understandable because the visible portions agree with one another.
Where the foreground and background have similar colors, separate them through ordinary optical cues.
A near edge may be sharper, a distant surface may receive softer light, and a contact shadow may reveal a small gap.
Do not draw an artificial bright outline around the subject.
If two dark forms overlap, allow some of that overlap to remain quiet rather than forcing every boundary to maximum contrast.
The most important contacts need clarity; less important background junctions can be ambiguous in the normal way a photographed place is ambiguous when viewed briefly.
Use negative space as part of the action's readability.
A hand needs a little clear area in the direction it is about to move, and a diving bird needs visible water below its perch.
This does not mean centering every object or distributing props symmetrically.
The free space should follow the scene's physical task.
When the action occupies that space, the composition can become denser for a moment and then open again during recovery.
Preserve the setting behind it so this change feels like movement through a place rather than a rearrangement of graphic elements.
The brightest region of the frame need not always be the protagonist.
A window, sky opening or lamp can be brighter while the subject remains readable through shape, placement and movement.
Control the size of those bright regions so they do not overwhelm the action.
A small reflection can attract the eye briefly and then recede as its angle changes.
Broad highlights should retain enough shape to identify their source.
Avoid automatic-looking exposure pumping that darkens a face whenever a reflective object passes through the composition.
Let shadows have different degrees of softness according to the light source and distance to the receiving surface.
A broad window gives a soft edge, while a small nearby lamp can make a more defined one.
Contact shadows are tighter than shadows cast across a larger gap.
On a curved receiver, the shadow changes shape with the surface.
If several sources contribute, their shadows can overlap with unequal darkness.
This physical variety helps explain depth without applying the same dark border to every object in the scene.
Reflected color should be local.
A warm wooden counter can return a little warmth to the underside of a hand above it.
Green foliage can tint a shaded patch near a stream.
Red task lighting can color nearby metal while a distant opening remains cool.
Keep these influences weaker than direct illumination unless the scene explicitly places the subject close to a large colored surface.
The reflected tint belongs to the facing side of an object and changes gradually with distance, rather than replacing the object's base color across its whole visible area.
Fine details should obey the scale of the view.
A close hand can show a crease near a knuckle, while a distant face needs only its stable overall proportions and expression.
The grain of a nearby wooden tool may be visible, but the far wall does not need equally sharp pores.
As the camera moves, details become available through a change of angle or distance rather than appearing as random new marks.
Preserve the few distinctive features that identify an object, and let less important texture merge naturally when it is too small to resolve.
When a reflective surface turns, its highlight can travel faster than a mark painted on it.
The highlight is an image of a light source seen through the changing surface orientation, while the mark belongs to the material.
Keep that distinction on wet clay, metal rims, glass and water.
A highlight may disappear at an angle where the source is no longer reflected.
It should not leave a permanent bright stain behind.
Conversely, a scratch or chip does not slide across the object merely because the camera changes position.
Translucent edges should retain their own thickness and texture.
A leaf against the light may show a warmer or brighter rim, and thin paper can glow softly near a lamp.
Steam can reveal an object behind it with reduced contrast.
These are different kinds of transmission and should not share one identical blur effect.
Keep opaque supports opaque.
A hand behind steam remains a solid hand glimpsed through moving vapor; it does not become transparent itself.
When the vapor clears, the same hand occupies the same physical place.
The action's pace should fit ordinary human or animal movement at its stated scale.
A small precise adjustment takes less travel than a broad gesture but can still have a deliberate beginning and ending.
Do not stretch a short line of dialogue into unnatural syllables merely to occupy the clip.
Let quiet anticipation and recovery provide breathing room where appropriate.
A fast event can happen within a calmer surrounding interval.
The scene's detail describes what is present during that interval, rather than requiring each noun to receive its own separate time allocation.
For scenes with speech, give the sentence an intention appropriate to the relationship.
A practical instruction can be clear without being stern; a question can be curious without sounding anxious; a calm reply can be warm without becoming sentimental.
Preserve the exact specified words while allowing natural stress, breath and a small pause where the phrase requires it.
The listener's response begins from understanding the line, not from mechanically copying the speaker's mouth.
Environmental sound continues underneath, maintaining the shared location of both people.
In scenes without speech, resist the urge to supply explanatory vocalizations.
The sound of an instrument, water, machinery or food cooking can make the action clear.
Silence from the visible subjects is compatible with a detailed active environment.
A small breath or ordinary incidental sound may belong naturally to a person, but it should not become a substitute narration.
The listener should be able to follow the relationship between motion and sound without being told what to notice by an unseen voice.
Maintain the distinction between a source moving and a listener moving.
During a small camera track, a stationary sound source can shift gently within the stereo field because the viewpoint changes.
It does not need to grow suddenly louder unless the camera actually approaches it substantially.
A moving source can change position while the environmental bed remains stable.
Keep those changes smooth and proportional to the visible distances.
Avoid a dramatic stereo sweep for an object that moves only a few centimeters within the shot.
Low sounds should carry weight without masking every other detail.
A motor hum or drum body can occupy the lower register while speech, contact sounds and air movement remain distinguishable above it.
The low component should not become a continuous cinematic rumble added to an otherwise ordinary place.
High sounds likewise need restraint: metallic jingles, a relay click or water spray can be crisp without piercing the mix.
The balance should resemble attentive listening near the scene, with enough dynamic room for a meaningful brief event to stand out.
The last audible decay can continue after the corresponding visible motion stops.
A resonant instrument, hard-surface tap or small splash leaves a short tail in its environment.
That tail should gradually reveal the quieter background already present underneath.
Do not cut every source off at the same instant or replace the ending with a generic fade.
Let the scene end naturally. Preserve the established framing and let the ambient sound continue.

## Harbor: the tide chart
The fabric cover around the folded tide chart is rust red, with a narrow border. This detail belongs to the existing object, stays at its established location and remains subordinate to the main action. Preserve its material and appearance through the camera movement.
The event takes place beside a small passenger ferry tied to a working harbor pier just before sunrise. An adult mechanic stands on the ferry's open side deck, and its captain stands beside the cabin entrance. The mechanic offers a folded tide chart and says, "The channel is clear." The captain accepts it, answers, "Then we can go," and looks out toward the harbor entrance. A slow lateral camera move reveals the channel beyond their shoulders. The boat remains moored throughout this brief exchange. Close voices, water against the hull, a loose halyard and a distant gull make the soundscape; there is no music.
The ferry is a practical coastal launch with a dark blue hull and a narrow cream band beneath its windows.
It carries a small enclosed cabin forward and an open passenger area behind it.
The camera is on the open deck, looking diagonally toward the cabin and the gap between the two people.
This angle places the pier along the left edge of the view and open water farther to the right.
The horizon is low enough that the upper part of the cabin has a clear silhouette against the pale sky.
Nothing in the composition suggests that the ferry is already underway.
The mechanic has finished a routine inspection rather than an emergency repair.
Their expression is alert but comfortable, with the slight tiredness of an early start.
They wear a plain work jacket over a warm shirt and carry no conspicuous badge or brand.
A few old creases in the jacket show where the elbows bend.
The sleeve nearest the chart has a darker damp patch near its cuff from resting against the rail.
Keep that patch in the same place as the arm moves.
The mechanic's free hand rests lightly on the top of a closed tool bag at hip level.
The captain is a different adult, dressed for a cool morning outside.
A heavy knit sweater is visible beneath an open weatherproof coat.
Their hair is tidy but not freshly styled, and the light catches a few loose strands when they turn toward the water.
Their stance is balanced on the gently moving deck, with one foot slightly ahead of the other.
They are listening to the mechanic before the first line begins.
The captain does not interrupt or make a broad theatrical gesture.
Their reply is a small decision shared between people accustomed to working together.
The tide chart is a real paper object with several old folds.

Faint printed lines and numbers are visible as a texture on its pale surface without becoming a readable title or a map inset.
A soft graphite mark near one fold suggests that it has been used for planning.
The mechanic holds its lower edge between the thumb and fingers, keeping the paper clear of the damp rail.
Its upper corner lifts slightly in the breeze before the captain takes it.
Begin with both people already in the frame.
The mechanic's hand and the chart occupy the space between their bodies, below their faces.
This arrangement lets the first line and the handover belong to the same view.

The captain's receiving hand rises from beside the coat, touches the opposite edge and supports it before the mechanic releases their grip.

The mechanic's line is spoken in an ordinary low voice suitable for the quiet morning. The consonants remain clear, but the delivery does not sound like a public announcement. Their mouth and jaw make the small movements of the exact words, and their eyes remain on the captain. There is a slight release of breath after "clear." The captain acknowledges the information with a very small nod before replying. The pause is long enough to register listening and short enough that the exchange feels familiar. Do not add another question, greeting or explanation of the voyage.

The head follows the eyes through a modest turn, revealing more of the cheek nearest the exterior light. The chart settles against the front of the coat, still visibly held. The mechanic follows the captain's look with a quieter change of attention. Both remain in place. The ending is anticipation of departure, not departure itself: no engine surge, released rope or sudden movement of the ferry is needed.
